title: Bits on the wire
summary: What voltage, photons, and radio actually carry your packet, and why the speed of light bounds everything above.
crux: What voltage, photons, and radio actually carry your packet, and why the speed of light bounds everything above.
keytakeaway: Every byte of Internet traffic travels as voltage on copper, light pulses through glass fibre, or modulated radio waves through air. The medium has a bandwidth (bits per second, determined by Shannon's theorem) and a propagation delay (length divided by signal speed, ~200,000 km/s in fibre). Higher protocols layer on top but cannot beat these physics — a New-York-to-Sydney request will always take at least ~200 ms round-trip. Practical engineering means knowing the floor numbers, recognising bandwidth-bound vs latency-bound problems, and applying the right fix: more parallelism / wider links / compression for bandwidth, or CDN edges / cache hits / round-trip elimination for latency.
misconceptions: Heads-up: bandwidth is not latency :: You cannot solve latency by buying bandwidth. A 10 Gb/s link doesn't move one byte faster than 100 Mb/s — bytes travel at light speed. More bandwidth increases throughput, not speed. Pre-position data (CDN) or eliminate round-trips (HTTP/2 push, QUIC 0-RTT, TLS resumption).

title: IP packets: addressed envelopes
summary: How a packet finds its way across millions of independent networks, what the IP header carries, and where datagrams die.
crux: How does a packet find a server when no router knows the full route?
keytakeaway: IP turns the Internet into a working system by addressing every packet with a 32-bit (IPv4) or 128-bit (IPv6) destination and letting each router make a local longest-prefix-match forwarding decision — no router knows the global path, yet millions of them cooperate via BGP and interior gateway protocols. Real-world operational concerns sit above the protocol: PMTUD black holes from filtered ICMP, BGP hijacks defeated only by RPKI deployment, NAT and CGNAT distorting end-to-end addressing, and DSCP / ECN markings that work inside one network but rarely survive the public Internet. Knowing the IP layer is what makes the network observable instead of mysterious.
misconceptions: Path MTU Discovery black-holes :: A router drops your packet and sends ICMP "packet too big," but a middlebox silently discards the ICMP. You never learn to shrink packets, retransmit at 1500 bytes forever, hitting ~1 second timeouts. TCP MSS clamping and assuming 1280-byte MTU mitigate this in practice.

title: The TCP handshake
summary: What SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK actually negotiate — and why a connection's first RTT decides the speed of every request on it.
crux: What SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK actually negotiate — and why a connection's first RTT decides the speed of every request on it.
keytakeaway: TCP's three-way handshake exchanges and acknowledges starting sequence numbers in both directions before any byte of application data flows, costing one full RTT per connection. Modern Linux protects the handshake with SYN cookies under flood, replaces the loss-based congestion control of Reno with CUBIC or BBR for lossy long-RTT paths, and uses RACK-TLP to detect loss faster than the classic RTO timer. Above the protocol layer the operational concerns are TIME-WAIT exhaustion (fix with connection pools + tcp_tw_reuse), Nagle/delayed-ACK stalls (fix with TCP_NODELAY), and kernel-tunable hygiene for any service handling thousands of handshakes per second.
misconceptions: Heads-up: SYN floods aren't dead :: SYN cookies mitigate classic SYN floods but ignore TCP options like timestamps. Modern attacks layer SYN floods with TLS ClientHellos, starving handshake CPU. Defence is layered: rate limits, connection priming, and abuse-pattern detection.

title: DNS: from name to address
summary: How a recursive resolver climbs the root → TLD → authoritative tree to turn google.com into an IP, and where caches and DNSSEC live.
crux: How a recursive resolver climbs the root → TLD → authoritative tree to turn `google.com` into an IP, and where caches and DNSSEC live.
keytakeaway: DNS is a globally distributed hierarchical key-value store mapping names to IP addresses (plus other record types). A recursive resolver walks the tree from root → TLD → authoritative on behalf of clients, caches results per record TTL, and returns the final answer. The operational frontier in 2026 is encrypted transports (DoH on 443, DoT on 853, DoQ on QUIC), authenticated responses via DNSSEC, and privacy-conscious choices around EDNS Client Subnet — every one of which trades a small amount of latency or geographic precision for confidentiality the original UDP/53 protocol never had.
misconceptions: Heads-up: TTL isn't security :: Low TTL does not prevent cache poisoning. Defences are randomized transaction IDs, random source ports, 0x20 case-mixing, and DNSSEC validation. TTL only controls stale data duration, not poisoning risk.

title: TLS 1.3: keys and confidentiality in one RTT
summary: How ClientHello key shares plus a certificate verifier collapse the old TLS 1.2 two-RTT handshake into one — and what 0-RTT actually buys you.
crux: How key shares and ECDHE collapse TLS 1.2's two-RTT handshake into one, and what 0-RTT buys you.
keytakeaway: TLS 1.3 collapses the handshake to one RTT by sending the client's ECDHE key share inside ClientHello, mandates ephemeral key exchange so every session has Perfect Forward Secrecy, and supports 0-RTT resumption — but 0-RTT must be restricted to idempotent methods or replay attacks turn the optimisation into a duplicate-write disaster. Above that protocol layer sits the post-2024 operational frontier: hybrid post-quantum key shares, Encrypted ClientHello, kernel-TLS offload, and CRLite-style revocation that finally replaces soft-fail OCSP.
misconceptions: Heads-up: 0-RTT replay :: 0-RTT data is not protected against replay attacks. An attacker on the wire can capture a 0-RTT ClientHello and resend it to the server. For idempotent requests (GET), that's benign; for state-changing requests (POST), that's exploitable. Server policy must restrict 0-RTT to safe HTTP methods.

title: HTTP/1.1, /2, /3: what changed and why
summary: Head-of-line blocking is the antagonist. Each version tries a different shape — pipelining, multiplexing on TCP, multiplexing on QUIC — to defeat it.
crux: Why each HTTP version exists, what each version changed, and why head-of-line blocking is the core antagonist.
keytakeaway: HTTP/1.1 multiplexes by opening six TCP connections; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection (but TCP head-of-line blocking still bites under loss); HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP and isolates loss to individual streams while adding connection migration for mobile. Above the protocol layer, the headers — Cache-Control, Authorization, CORS, SameSite cookies, ETag, Priority — are where most operational bugs live and most security wins or losses happen. Modern production HTTP means serving all three versions, choosing per-connection via ALPN, and monitoring HTTP/3 fallback rate as a leading indicator of network-path health.
misconceptions: Heads-up: HTTP/2 ≠ HOL-free :: HTTP/2 multiplexes at the HTTP layer, but sits on TCP — an ordered byte stream. One lost TCP packet stalls all HTTP/2 streams. Only HTTP/3 (with QUIC) escapes HOL blocking at the transport layer.

title: CDN: serving bytes from close
summary: How an Anycast IP, a smart DNS, and a tiered cache cooperate so the response comes from 20 ms away instead of 200 ms.
crux: How CDN caching defeats latency: edge locations, cache keys, and why forgetting `Vary` breaks everything.
keytakeaway: A CDN turns "the server is 250 ms away" into "the server is 20 ms away" by replicating content to hundreds of edge POPs and routing each user to the nearest via Anycast or GeoDNS. The interesting layer is cache configuration — Cache-Control TTLs, Vary header keying, surgical purges via cache-tags, edge-side composition for partially-cacheable pages, and stale-while-revalidate for graceful misses. Most CDN-related production incidents trace back to one of three causes: missing Vary (cache poisoning across users), wrong Vary (cache fragmenting per User-Agent), or the deploy pipeline not purging on origin updates.
misconceptions: Heads-up: cookies aren't in the cache key by default :: CDNs cache by URL and headers in the `Vary` response. Cookies are NOT in the cache key. If your endpoint reads cookies, mark it `private` (no CDN cache) or add `Vary: Cookie` — else one user's page serves to another.

title: WebSocket and real-time
summary: How a single persistent TCP connection becomes a full-duplex message pipe — and why applications still crash when clients can't keep up.
crux: How a single persistent TCP connection becomes a full-duplex message pipe — and why applications still crash when clients can't keep up.
keytakeaway: WebSocket converts a request-response connection into a bidirectional message pipe. The handshake is HTTP; the payload is a compact binary frame format. The hard part is not the protocol — it is managing backpressure when clients can't keep up, handling reconnection without loss, and scaling to millions of connections across regions. Monitor slow-client count and per-connection queue depth; they are your early warning before cascading failure.

title: QUIC internals
summary: How QUIC merges UDP, transport logic, and TLS into a fast, multiplexed protocol that runs entirely in user space and survives network path changes.
crux: How QUIC merges UDP, transport logic, and TLS into a fast protocol that multiplexes streams and survives network migration.
keytakeaway: QUIC fuses UDP, TLS 1.3, and transport multiplexing into a user-space protocol that completes its handshake in 1 RTT (vs TCP+TLS 2–3 RTT), eliminates head-of-line blocking via independent streams (575× latency improvement on lossy paths), and survives network migration via connection IDs. The trade-off is CPU cost (15–30% higher per byte than kernel TCP, up to ~45% goodput loss on fast links). Deployment is phased: mobile clients benefit from QUIC's latency and HoL elimination; desktop and high-throughput paths remain TCP. UDP blocking in ~3–5% of networks requires mandatory fallback to HTTP/2. Operationally, QUIC encryption breaks traditional packet inspection, demanding application-level observability and tracing infrastructure. The protocol is now 5 years old (RFC 9000, 2021) with ~21% web-traffic adoption, ~35–40% of major sites advertising support, and steady growth as client implementations mature and hardware offload reduces CPU cost.
misconceptions: Heads-up: QUIC is fragile to UDP blocking :: 3–5% of networks block UDP outright. When silently dropped, QUIC times out and falls back to HTTP/2, adding latency. Browsers race QUIC and TCP in parallel, so whichever succeeds first wins. Fallback to HTTP/2 must be seamless.

title: Network security
summary: How networks are attacked by volumetric floods, state exhaustion, and application-layer exploits — and how engineers defend with rate limiting, mTLS, and defense-in-depth architecture.
crux: How DDoS attacks work and how to defend with rate limiting, firewalls, WAFs, and anycast scrubbing centers.
keytakeaway: Network security requires defending three attack vectors: volumetric floods (L3/L4) absorbed at the CDN edge via stateless rate limiting and anycast distribution; protocol exhaustion (SYN floods, RST injection) blocked by kernel mitigations (SYN cookies, RFC 5961 challenge-ACK); and application-layer attacks (HTTP floods, Slowloris, expensive queries) detected by WAFs and rate limiters tuned to your traffic patterns. Defense architecture is layered (edge → gateway → origin) and operational (detect anomalies, tune rules, escalate to humans). The economics favor the attacker only if you defend alone; CDNs amortize cost across customers and make DDoS uneconomical.
misconceptions: Heads-up: amplification is the economist's choice for attackers :: Botnets cost ~$50-500/month. Amplification attacks cost nothing: send one query, get 50x amplified response. DNS open-resolvers, NTP servers, and misconfigured memcached are free weapons. That is why they are targeted constantly.

title: Putting it together: one HTTPS request, end to end
summary: All twelve layers — from DNS through security gates to browser render — orchestrate in 200-400 ms. Walk one HTTPS request end to end, encounter proxy defenses, QUIC optimizations, and WebSocket detours. Then use the budget sandbox to decide where time goes.
crux: When you type a URL and the page loads, which twelve things happen in order, and where does the 200–400 ms go?
keytakeaway: Every HTTPS request is a coordinated sequence of twelve layers: DNS to find the IP, TCP for reliable byte transport, load balancers and proxies for health checks and routing, TLS for confidentiality and integrity (plus optional mTLS for service-to-service), rate limiters and WAFs for security, HTTP for application-level conversation, QUIC for low-latency alternatives and connection migration, WebSocket upgrades for real-time bidirectional flows, CDN edges for geographic proximity and cache, routers for packet forwarding, and the browser's render pipeline. Optimisation work means knowing which layer dominates each specific slow request — round-trip elimination (cache hits, 0-RTT, connection migration) is the highest-leverage move; round-trip shortening (CDN, multi-region, edge compute) is next; everything within a round-trip (compression, parsing speed, smaller bundles) is third. Security hardening (mTLS for service mesh, WAF for edge, rate limiting for DDoS) must not be retrofitted; design it in from layer 1. The operational frontier is distributed tracing with W3C Trace Context, USE/RED method-based instrumentation, circuit breakers for cascade isolation, and error-budget-driven release cadence — all of which give you the vocabulary to debug, design, and ship performant, resilient network-bound systems.
misconceptions: Heads-up: cascading retries amplify outages across all 12 layers :: Retry storms amplify outages. Origin timeout causes retries at every layer. A 99.9% server sees 10× normal load in 30s from cascading retries. Defense: exponential backoff + jitter, circuit breakers, load shedding, bulkheads.
